name: Making Testing Fair and Scientifically Sound
gist: Papers improve how benchmarks are scored and designed so results are reproducible, reliable, and reveal genuine progress rather than just progress on specific test data.
explain: A benchmark that is flawed in its design can lead you to the wrong conclusions. If you score a benchmark in a biased way, you reward some kinds of answers over others unequally. If your test data happens to match one model's training style better than another—such as lots of examples exactly like its training data—that model will look better even if it is not genuinely better overall in real situations it has not seen. If your benchmark is too easy or too hard, you might think a model is better or worse than it really is, because easy tests hide the real limitations while hard tests hide genuine progress. This subtheme is about the scientific process of benchmarking itself: making sure tests are fair, reproducible, and actually measure what they claim to measure.

The difficulty is subtle. Benchmarks can fail in ways that are not obvious. Maybe your benchmark has data leakage: examples that accidentally got into both training and test data, which makes models look better than they are because they memorized that specific data. Maybe you scored answers in a way that favors certain models by accident, such as giving credit for partially correct answers when one type of model tends to be partially correct while another type tends to be very wrong or very right, which means the scoring rules accidentally help one model family. Maybe your test is so hard that all models fail equally, telling you nothing about relative progress, or so easy that all models pass, hiding real differences. Maybe you reported the top score without showing all the scores across models, giving a misleading picture. Scientific benchmarking requires careful thinking about these details.

Researchers working on this focus on fundamentals of good testing: How should you split data between training and testing to avoid leakage? How should you measure fairness so that results are not biased toward one model or approach? How should you report results to be honest and reproducible? How should you track whether a benchmark is actually useful or whether models have learned to game it in ways that do not transfer to real-world tasks? The papers here often reveal that popular benchmarks have these problems, which means people using those benchmarks may be making the wrong conclusions about which models are actually better. Researchers then propose concrete changes to benchmark design—different data splits, different scoring rules, different reporting practices—that prevent these errors. This work is less flashy than building a new benchmark, but it is essential for honest science.

papers.title: Benchmarking Stochastic Approximation Algorithms for Fairness-Constrained Training of Deep Neural Networks
papers.contribution: Establishes benchmark for comparing fairness-constrained learning algorithms in terms of optimization performance and fairness improvement.

papers.title: CTBench: Cryptocurrency Time Series Generation Benchmark
papers.contribution: First cryptocurrency benchmark systematizing 452-token dataset evaluation across eight TSG methods, revealing trade-offs between statistical quality and trading profitability.

papers.title: RankLLM: Weighted Ranking of LLMs by Quantifying Question Difficulty
papers.contribution: Achieves 90% agreement with human judgments on 30 models and 35,550 questions, demonstrating stability, fast convergence, and computational efficiency.

papers.title: The Illusion of Generalization in Tabular Language Models
papers.contribution: Binary/categorical classification achieve near-zero median lift; instruction-tuning recovers 92.2% of performance, suggesting claimed generalization reflects evaluation artifacts.

papers.title: USTBench: Benchmarking and Dissecting Spatiotemporal Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs as Urban Agents
papers.contribution: Evaluation of 14 leading LLMs reveals they struggle in long-horizon planning and reflective adaptation; reasoning models don't consistently outperform non-reasoning LLMs.

papers.title: AI Cartography: Mapping the Latent Landscape of AI Benchmark Ecosystems
papers.contribution: Reveals local dependence among benchmarks, shows contributor metadata explains more rank variance than architecture, identifies reliable latent general-factor vs unreliable manifest slopes.

papers.title: Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks
papers.contribution: ATLAS reduces required items by up to 90% while maintaining measurement precision and detecting meaningful ability differences among models with identical accuracies.

papers.title: BRIDGE: Predicting Human Task Completion Time From Model Performance
papers.contribution: Infers human task completion time for new benchmarks from model performance; reproduces METR's exponential scaling with 50% horizon doubling every 6 months.

papers.title: Beyond Benchmarks: Toward Causally Faithful Evaluation of Large Language Models
papers.contribution: The framework enables more interpretable, reproducible, and carefully attributed assessment of model capability by probing dataset-induced effects and jointly modeling evaluation components.

papers.title: Choices Speak Louder than Questions
papers.contribution: NPSQ demonstrates stability across various input formats (cloze, symbols, hybrid) while traditional scoring methods remain vulnerable to superficial characteristics of answer choices.

papers.title: DM4CT: Benchmarking Diffusion Models for Computed Tomography Reconstruction
papers.contribution: Provides detailed insights into diffusion model behavior for CT reconstruction; a public real-world high-resolution synchrotron dataset enables rigorous evaluation.

papers.title: Diagnosing the Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge via Item Response Theory
papers.contribution: Leveraging IRT-GRM yields interpretable signals for diagnosing LLM judge reliability systematically and identifying potential causes of unreliability.

papers.title: EEG-FM-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for the Systematic Evaluation and Diagnostic Analyses of EEG Foundation Models
papers.contribution: Reveals that multi-task learning acts as regularizer in data-scarce EEG contexts, gradient conflicts limit pre-training efficiency, and objective alignment is critical.

papers.title: FLIP2: Expanding Protein Fitness Landscape Benchmarks for Real-World Machine Learning Applications
papers.contribution: Reveals simpler models often outperform fine-tuned protein language models, challenging utility of existing transfer learning techniques.

papers.title: How NOT to benchmark your SITE metric: Beyond Static Leaderboards and Towards Realistic Evaluation.
papers.contribution: Reveals that simple dataset-agnostic heuristics can outperform sophisticated methods on current benchmarks, highlighting a disconnect from real-world complexity.

papers.title: ImagenWorld: Stress-Testing Image Generation Models with Explainable Human Evaluation on Open-ended Real-World Tasks
papers.contribution: Comprehensive evaluation of 14 models reveals models struggle more in editing than generation, excel in artistic domains but struggle with symbolic/text-heavy content.

papers.title: InteractComp: Evaluating Search Agents With Ambiguous Queries
papers.contribution: Reveals striking failure with best model achieving only 13.73% despite 71.50% with complete context, with forced interaction producing dramatic gains and demonstrating latent capability.

papers.title: Item Response Scaling Laws: A Measurement Theory Approach for Efficient and Generalizable Neural Scaling Estimation
papers.contribution: Achieves reliable scaling estimates with only 50 questions per benchmark (99.9% reduction) after one-time calibration, with generalizable model ability estimates.

papers.title: SAIR: Enabling Deep Learning for Protein-Ligand Interactions with a Synthetic Structural Dataset
papers.contribution: SAIR provides the largest publicly available dataset of protein-ligand structures with activity annotations and establishes benchmarks showing machine learning models outperform traditional scoring functions, though neither exhibit high correlation with ground

papers.title: When AI Benchmarks Plateau: A Systematic Study of Benchmark Saturation
papers.contribution: Finds nearly half of benchmarks exhibit saturation, increasing with age; expert-curated benchmarks resist saturation better than crowdsourced ones, while data privacy shows no protective effect.
